title: Chapter 179 – Yue's Bell
html:
[The Dock, Below the Gate Stair – Yue]

Yue has not heard a sound since she was nine years old, and she has never once been alone with the quiet.

It is always full. That is what the hearing do not understand when they pity her. The silence is not empty. It is crowded, thick as river water, and moves with a pulse of its own. She feels the stone under her feet breathe. She feels the heartbeat of the person beside her, a small hot knock against her ribs. She feels the long low tremor of the mountain, the one the hearing call quiet, and she knows it better than they know their own mothers' voices.

Tonight the tremor has a shape.

She sits on the cold stone of the Dock with her back against the Gate wall and her hand flat on the Pebble, and she feels the shape come up through the floor. It is wide. It is slow. It is like a very large animal turning over in a bed, shifting its weight onto the side that hurts, and every time it moves, the Pebble in her lap gives a small warm shudder, like a living thing flinching from a blow.

Heavy, she signs to nobody. Heavy tonight.

Beside her, on a folded cloak, Lin Kuang wakes with a start. He is thirteen, long-boned, all knees and elbows, and he has slept three hours in two days. His hand goes to the wooden sword on his chest. His eyes find her face, and she watches him read it, the way he has learned to, the small tightening at the corners of her mouth.

Again? he signs. His fingers are clumsy but quick.

She nods.

How bad?

She considers. She takes his hand and presses it flat on the stone beside hers, and lets him feel it. His eyes go wide. He snatches the hand back, rubbing the palm against his tunic as if burned.

Oh, he signs.

Yes.

What is it?

She does not know. But the Pebble does. She lifts it from her lap, a gray, cracked, ordinary-looking stone no bigger than a loaf, and holds it against her breastbone, and shuts her eyes, and listens the way she was taught.

* * *

The Pebble does not speak. It has no mouth.

What it does is lend her its ears. It has done so since she was a child of seven, a little deaf girl with a pocketful of river-stones, who found one that was warm. The warm one hummed. It hummed in a rhythm she could feel against her palm, and when she held it to her cheek, the rhythm changed to a shape, and the shape had meaning. A gate shut here. A stranger waited there. A grandfather was about to die. Pebble told her all of it. And when the fever took her hearing, at nine, the stone was already in her hand, and it simply kept talking.

She has never explained this to anyone. How would she? The rock tells me things. The hearing would say she was mad. Only Jian, who is always a little mad himself, ever asked the right question. He asked, What does it say tonight? And she told him.

Tonight it says: Door.

It says it in a low steady pulse, again and again, the way a heart says beat. A door is being pushed. Below, deep below, below the Dock and the Gate wall and the foot of the world, there is a door that has been closed for ten thousand years, and the Pebble has been holding it shut with all its strength since the first night.

The door is very old. The thing pushing it is very patient.

She opens her eyes.

"Yue." It is Tian Mo, standing over her, in the faint blue glow of the last working lamp. She does not hear him. She reads it on his lips, as she has read his lips for twenty years, the slow heavy movements of a man who does not like to waste a word. He is on one knee. His face is gray, the skin of it pulled tight over the bone. His left sleeve hangs empty and neatly pinned to the shoulder.

You should be resting, she signs at him.

His mouth twitches. You should be.

I am resting.

You are holding up a mountain.

It's a small mountain.

He laughs. She feels the laugh, a dry puff of breath against her fingers, and it warms her more than she expected.

Come, he signs. The Dock. Something has come.

* * *

On the stair, Tian Mo tells her about the arm.

He does it without being asked, in the long dim stretch between the fourth and fifth landings, with one hand on the rail and his pinned sleeve swinging. He speaks aloud, slowly, so she can read him. She does not interrupt.

"It did not hurt," he says. "That is what surprised me. I thought a limb torn off would be the worst pain of my life. It was only pressure. A huge, slow squeeze, and then a kind of quiet. The roots had already come. They bound it before the blood could run. A man named Dai, one of my guards, tied the cord." He stops. "I looked down and saw it was gone and felt, for a moment, nothing at all. And then I felt very ashamed."

Why?

"Because I had been proud of the stair. Twenty-three years, and I thought it was my doing." His mouth twists. "It was the tree. It was the roots. It was Dai with his cord and the stone creature that gave a hand to save my life. All I did was stand. Anyone can stand."

Not anyone, Yue signs.

"No?"

I have watched people try. They don't. She touches his sleeve, where it is pinned. You stayed after it took your arm. You did not retreat. That is not anyone.

He is silent a long moment. Then he lifts his one hand and presses it, very briefly, against hers.

"I think I will like having only one arm to hold a staff with," he says, and for the first time in two days, he smiles.

* * *

The Dock is the lowest place in the Garden, a vast black cavern at the foot of the Gate stair, and it has not been used for anything but ghosts in a thousand years.

It is round. Its floor is a polished disc of black stone sixty paces across, with a seam at the center where the Gate wall rises, a sheer cliff of the same stone, unmarked and featureless, thirty feet high. A ring of blue lamps burns along the wall, most of them guttering. At the cavern's mouth, where the stair arrives, a handful of guards stand with spears, watching the dark. A smell rolls out of the tunnel, a cold iron breath.

Yue stands beside Tian Mo and watches what has come.

It is a herd.

She has never seen so many Gnashers in one place. They fill the great tunnel beyond the Dock, the old Shaft the Founders cut, wall to wall and nose to tail, a river of dark gray hide and bone-plated jaws. They are not attacking. They have come to the mouth of the cavern and stopped, as cows stop at a gate. A thousand heavy heads are lifted toward the Gate wall. A thousand pairs of small red eyes are fixed on a place about ten feet above the floor.

They are waiting, Tian Mo signs.

For what?

I don't know. The guards say they came an hour ago. They have not moved. He hesitates. Yue. I think they are listening.

She frowns. Then she understands. She lays her palm against the black wall of the Gate and feels it, as she felt it through the floor: the deep slow pulse of the door, and beneath it a second, quicker pulse, answering. It comes from the herd. Every beast in the tunnel is breathing in time with the thing behind the Gate.

One of the guards, a short stout woman named Dai, is standing at the front of the line with her spear in both hands. She is shaking. Yue can see it from here, the fine tremor of the shaft against the stone. But she does not move. She has been told to hold the Dock, and the Dock is what she is holding, though it is full of an army she cannot possibly stop.

Yue crosses to her and lays a hand on her arm. Dai looks round, startled. Her face is sweaty, round, ordinary. She has a tiny scar over one eyebrow and a smear of soot on her chin.

"Mistress Yue." The lips move. "I'm not afraid."

Good, Yue signs, and then, because she is not sure Dai can read it, she smiles and pats the arm twice, the way she would a nervous horse.

Dai laughs, a short cracked laugh. "That's a lie," she says, and Yue reads it plainly. "But thank you. I will remember that someone patted my arm when the end of the world came. It is more than most people get."

They are being called, she signs.

By what?

By the thing that is pushing.

She turns to him. His face, in the lamplight, is very still.

Tian Mo, she signs. When the Pebble is cracked, the door will open.

How long?

A day. Perhaps less.

And then?

Then they go in. All of them. And whatever is on the other side comes out.

* * *

It is Lin Kuang who finds the bell.

He has followed them down, of course, because he is thirteen and no order in the world can keep him from a thing that looks dangerous. He stands at the edge of the Dock with his wooden sword in his belt and his mouth open, staring up at the vault. She follows his gaze. And there, in the dim shadow of the roof, hanging from a bracket of black iron on a chain as thick as her wrist, is something she has seen all her life and never looked at.

It is a bell. Bronze, green with age, as tall as a man. No clapper. No rope. A dark rough surface worn smooth by a thousand years of damp, with a ring of characters cut round the lip in a script that Pei An once told her was older than the Sect.

What is it? Kuang signs.

A bell, she signs back.

I know it's a bell. Why is it here?

She does not know. She stands for a long moment with the Pebble pressed to her chest. And then, very slowly, the stone does something it has never done in all the years she has held it. It turns. In her hands, against her heart, it rolls an inch toward the bell, like a compass needle finding north.

Tian Mo has seen it too. His eyes narrow.

The Founders' bell, he signs. It was rung once, in the old stories. When the first Gate-Keeper closed the door. They said the sound turned the beasts back.

Turned them?

Made them stop. Made them go home. His jaw tightens. I always thought it was a story.

How was it rung?

It had no clapper. He looks at it, a long hard look. They said it was rung by a voice.

Yue's hand goes still on the stone.

A voice, she signs.

Yes.

I don't have one.

I know.

She stares at the bell. The shape of it hangs over her in the dimness, vast and green and silent, with its ring of characters and its dark open mouth, and she thinks of the sound it would make. She has never heard a bell. She does not know what it is like. She knows only what the hearing say: a long deep note that goes through the body and out the other side.

I could make a shape, she signs, slowly. If I had the sound.

What do you mean?

Pebble knows how. I would give it a hand and a voice. I would stand under the bell and let it ring through me. She looks at him. It would crack the stone. Maybe break it.

Tian Mo's face does not change. But she sees his one good hand curl slowly into a fist.

Then we find another way.

There isn't one.

We will think.

There is no time to think.

He is silent a long moment. Then, with enormous effort, he says it aloud, and she reads it off his lips: "I will not ask you to."

You are not asking, she signs. I am telling you.

* * *

Lin Kuang is waiting for her at the first landing, with his arms folded and his chin out.

He has been thinking. She can see it in the set of his shoulders, the way a boy of thirteen thinks, which is mostly by scowling. He does not sign. He speaks aloud, slowly, with the exaggerated care he has learned for her sake.

"You are going to do it."

Yes.

"Then I am coming."

No.

"You need someone to hold the Pebble if your hands go. You need someone to catch you if you fall." He sets his jaw. "You can't make me stay behind. Uncle Jian said I was to do what I thought was right, when it came to it. I think this is right."

Yue looks at him for a long while. She sees the shape of his father in him, and his grandmother's stubbornness, and something else, something new and grave and a little frightening, that she did not see a month ago. He has grown. They have all grown, and not one of them asked to.

Then you will stand behind me, she signs. You will not touch the bell. Whatever happens.

I promise.

Say it again.

"I promise," says Kuang, and for once he does not look away.

She takes his chin and kisses his forehead, hard, the way her mother did, and sends him up to find his sword. He goes at a run. She watches him go and presses her hand flat to her ribs, where the old stone is warm and heavy and beginning, very faintly, to ache.

* * *

She goes up the stair first, to say goodbye.

She does not call it that. Seven hundred and one steps, the long way, at the speed of a woman of seventy-one who has not slept, and she stops at every landing to breathe. The blue lamps are low. The roots in the walls are pale and still. At the top, the Garden Hall is full of light, the strange hard festival light Qinghe has lit, and it smells of porridge and lamp oil and three thousand sleepers.

Qinghe is at the kettle. She looks up and sees Yue's face, and her own goes white and then very gentle.

How long? she signs.

Dawn.

What will it cost?

Yue looks at her mother's hands. They are old, scarred, strong, with a burn on the left thumb from yesterday's bread. She has watched these hands sign to her for sixty years, every gesture patient, every letter shaped just so, because her mother learned a language for a deaf daughter before she had finished grieving the loss of the hearing one.

I don't know, she signs. Maybe the Pebble. Maybe my hands.

Qinghe does not argue. She pours tea. She sets the cup in front of her daughter and sits down opposite, and for a while they drink in silence, two women at a scarred kitchen table in a lit-up house at the end of the world.

When you were small, Qinghe signs at last, you used to put your hand on the pot to feel the water boil. I told you not to. You burned yourself twice.

I remember.

I thought, she will never learn. A faint wry twist of the mouth. You learned. You just wanted to feel it in your own way.

Mother.

Go, signs Qinghe. Do what you must. I will keep the kettle on.

It is all she says. It is all she needs to say. Yue kisses her forehead, and Qinghe holds her face between her two hard dry palms for a long moment, and lets her go.

On the way down, Feng stops her at the corner. He is leaning on the wall with his hand pressed flat to the stone and his eyes closed. He opens them, and she sees something wild and gentle in his face.

"The sound," he says aloud. She reads it with difficulty. "When you ring it. Will it be a long note?"

Yes.

"Then I'll hear it," he says, and grins. "Right through the wall. I always hear the long ones." He pats the stone. "Tell it I said thank you."

She does not know what he means. She nods anyway.

* * *

They do it at dawn.

She asks Lin Kuang to stay behind, and he refuses, and she lets him. She asks Tian Mo to go back up the stair, and he refuses, and she lets him too. Six guards, then, and the boy, and the old stone, and herself. They climb the iron scaffold to the underside of the bell, a hundred rungs in the dark, and Tian Mo comes after her one-handed, gray-faced, cursing silently with each step. They stand on a narrow platform under the green bronze, and the great cold shape hangs over them like a held breath.

Are you afraid? Kuang signs.

Yes.

Me too.

Good. She touches his cheek. Afraid people are careful.

She sets the Pebble against the underside of the bell, where the bronze is thinnest. She puts both palms on it. She closes her eyes. And she reaches for the thing she does only when she is alone and no one can see.

She opens the door in herself.

It is a small door. She found it when she was nine, in the week the fever took her hearing: a narrow dark gap in the back of her mind, where the missing sound used to be. It does not lead anywhere. It is only the place where the music would have gone. For sixty years she has kept it shut, because it hurts, because looking into it is like looking into a well of her own loss. But the Pebble knows how to fill it. And tonight, for the first time, she lets it.

The Pebble pours in.

It is not a sound. It is a wave. It comes up through her palms and into her wrists, and her elbows, and her chest, a vast warm golden pressure, as of a hand closing round her heart. Everything she cannot hear rushes into the silence at once. The Dock's old echo. The scrape of boots. The hum of the herd. The slow heavy heartbeat of the thing behind the door. She hears it all, every note at once, and it is the most beautiful and the most terrible thing she has ever felt.

And she hears.

She hears the first thing she ever heard, a woman's voice, her mother's, singing over a cradle. She hears her father's laugh. She hears Jian at twelve, shouting from a tree. She hears every sound of the first nine years of her life, replayed in a single heartbeat, bright and sharp and small, and she understands that the Pebble is not giving her sound. It is returning it. All the music she lost is still there, folded in the dark, kept by a stone through sixty years of silence.

It is the kindest thing anyone has ever done for her, and she has to spend it at once.

Now, she thinks. Ring.

She opens her mouth.

She has no voice. But the Pebble has one. It leaps through her throat like a spark through dry grass, a single clear unbroken tone, rising from the base of her spine and up and out through her teeth, and the bell above her answers.

The bronze moves.

It shivers. It sings. It lifts a note of such terrible purity that the iron scaffold rings with it, and the lamps flare white, and the guards on the platform fall to their knees with their hands over their ears. The note goes out. It pours across the Dock and through the tunnel and into the dark beyond, and she feels it hit the herd like the flat of a hand.

A thousand Gnashers lift their heads.

She feels them hear. She feels the whole vast mass of them go still, and then shudder, and then, one by one, begin to turn. It is a slow sweep, a great dark wheel pivoting in the narrow throat of the tunnel. They are not frightened. They are relieved. The command she gave them, the old Founders' command, the voice that closed the door ten thousand years ago, is a thing they know in their bones. It is a mother calling the herd home.

Go, sings the bell. Go back. It is not time. The door is closed.

They go.

She stands on the scaffold with her hands on the Pebble and her mouth open and tears running down her face and watches a thousand beasts file back up the dark tunnel, heavy-headed and docile, like cattle at dusk.

Beside her, Lin Kuang is laughing and crying. Tian Mo has gone down on his knees. Even the guards, deaf from the note, are grinning like boys.

It worked, Kuang signs wildly. It worked, it worked, Aunt Yue, it worked!

She does not answer. She cannot. The note is still going. She cannot stop it. It pours out of her, endless, golden, and it is growing, and she knows with a slow cold clarity that the bell is no longer answering the Pebble. It has become something else. The Pebble is no longer lending. It is spending.

She looks down.

A hairline crack has opened across the stone. It runs from one edge to the other, thin as a spider's thread, glowing gold from within.

Stop, she signs, with her one free hand. Stop. Stop.

But the bell does not stop, and the Pebble does not stop, and the crack widens.

It is the herd that sees it first. A thousand beasts, far up the tunnel, check in their stride and turn their heads. They have heard something. Not the bell. Something deeper. A sound she cannot hear and can feel in every bone of her body, the sound of a very old lock giving way.

Behind her, the Gate wall begins to open.

It does so without sound. A seam appears in the black stone, a hand's breadth wide, running from the floor to the height of a man, and from it a faint cold light spills out across the Dock. It is not blue. It is not gold. It is the pale gray color of a very early morning, and it carries a smell she has never smelled, dry and sweet and ancient, like pages in a closed book.

Something moves in the seam.

She sees it over Kuang's shoulder, over the shaking guards, over the glowing crack in the Pebble. A pale shape. Slender. Upright. It steps into the light and stands a moment with its head tilted, listening to the last echo of the bell die in the vault. It is the height of a child.

It lifts a hand, and waves.

Yue does not hear what it says. But she reads its lips, small, clear, polite, in the gray light of the door, and her blood runs cold.

Hello, it says. I have been waiting a very long time.
